title: The development of doctrine
hook: Newman: living ideas grow like a tree, staying themselves

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Henry Newman, later a priest of the Oratory, on a ship with no wind. Your line was lead, kindly light. What was your one next step? Today, the question Newman was wrestling with when he turned. Day eight hundred ninety.

An old photograph: a child on a doorstep, gap-toothed, in a too-big sweater. Then a photograph of the same person decades later. Hardly a feature is the same. The height, the face, the voice, all different. And yet nobody at the family table doubts that it's the same person. Something stayed while everything grew. Newman put a question like that to the whole Church. The Christians of the first generations didn't use every word the Church uses now. So is today's Church a different thing wearing an old name? Or the same thing, grown up?
screen: `A CHILD, THEN A GROWN ADULT.` → `THE SAME PERSON?` → `THE SAME CHURCH?`

segments.voice: Newman wrote a long book about it, An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, and was writing it in the months before he became Catholic. His answer comes in four parts. First, the problem. Some teachings were said in words the first Christians never used. The creed says the Son is of one substance with the Father. That phrase isn't in the Gospels. Did the Church add something new, or put into words what was there all along? Second, the image. A living idea, Newman argued, grows the way living things grow. A seed becomes a tree. Jesus himself compares the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed that grows into a tree where birds come to rest. The tree looks nothing like the seed, yet it is the same plant, and no other plant could come from that seed. Third, the sentence. Newman wrote: "In a higher world it is otherwise, but here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often." Notice what that does not say. It does not say anything goes. Fourth, the test. Newman knew that ideas can also decay, the way a body can sicken instead of grow. So he tried to describe how to tell a true development from a corruption: a true one keeps the same type, the same principles, and it carries forward what came before instead of overturning it. Catholic teaching today speaks of doctrine developing in this sense. Other Christians describe faithfulness over time in their own ways, and they have their own words for it. For Newman, the question was not whether the Church had changed. It was whether it had stayed itself while growing.
screen: `WORDS THE FIRST CHRISTIANS NEVER USED.` · `A SEED BECOMES A TREE.` · `HERE BELOW TO LIVE IS TO CHANGE.` · `GROWTH, OR DECAY?` · then, large: `TO BE PERFECT IS TO HAVE CHANGED OFTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how your own faith, or your own deepest convictions, have grown. Settle, and breathe. Think back to how you understood God, or goodness, or what matters, when you were a child. A picture, a prayer, a rule. Now set it next to how you understand it today. What has changed? And what, under all that change, has stayed the same? Don't judge either one. If you pray, you can give thanks for the growth. If you don't, simply notice the thread that runs from then to now. The bell holds the time.
Mustard seed. The image Jesus used for a growing kingdom, which Newman borrowed to explain how a true teaching can grow into something unrecognizable and still be the same plant.
Your line: to live is to change. Today, look at something you once held tightly and now hold differently, and ask what stayed the same under the change. Day eight hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Catholic theologians and teachers draw on Newman's idea of development when they explain how the Church's teaching is put into new words over the centuries while remaining faithful to what was handed down.

fork.setup: you notice the Church now uses words the first Christians never used. what do you conclude, with Newman?
options: the Church has become something else.
a living idea grows, and can stay itself while growing.
fork.reveal: Newman argued that living ideas grow like a seed into a tree, and offered ways to tell growth from decay.

trapdoor: what you thought: doctrine is a fixed list that never moves.
what it means: Newman argued that a living teaching grows, like a seed becoming a tree, while keeping the same type and principles.
what a scholar hears: Newman tried to set out tests for telling a true development from a corruption, and his Essay was written as he moved toward the Catholic Church.

notes: Claims rule: the number of Newman's 'notes' of a true development is left out; the script names only same type, same principles and continuity. Confirm wording.
'Finished it in the months before he became Catholic': confirm (Newman left the Essay unfinished as he was received).
The oak/seed image is the script's illustration of Newman's growth analogy; Newman's own images in the Essay include a stream and the growth of the body. Confirm acceptable.
Exact wording of the Newman quotation: confirm against the 1845 or 1878 edition.
The sentence on other Christians is kept deliberately neutral; check it is fair.

Editor pass: 'finished it' changed to 'was writing it' (the Essay was broken off and published after his reception); the mixed mustard-seed/oak image fixed; 'Catholics today speak' changed to 'Catholic teaching today speaks'; replaced the repeated 'turns four ways' opener.
